prompt: Write an essay of at least 900 words on the topic of navigable freeway. Make sure the entire response is in English and no capital letters are used.
response:
the concept of a navigable freeway is one that sits at the intersection of engineering, urban planning, and human psychology. at first glance, the phrase seems almost redundant. a freeway, by definition, is a road designed for high-speed travel, with no traffic lights, no cross streets, and no pedestrians. it is meant to be driven, not navigated in the sense of a winding country lane. yet the word “navigable” introduces a crucial nuance. a freeway can be physically passable but cognitively or emotionally unnavigable. it can exist as concrete and asphalt, yet fail as a system that a driver can understand, predict, and use without stress. a truly navigable freeway is therefore not just a strip of pavement; it is a carefully choreographed environment that respects human limits while enabling efficient movement.

to understand what makes a freeway navigable, we must first consider the basic elements of wayfinding. on any road, a driver needs three things: a clear sense of current position, a reliable prediction of what comes next, and a low-effort way to execute lane changes, exits, and merges. on a poorly designed freeway, these three elements break down. signs are placed too late or too densely. lanes end without warning. exits are numbered inconsistently. the result is a phenomenon familiar to any commuter: the sudden, panicked swerve across three lanes because the driver only just realized the exit was upon them. such a freeway is technically open, but it is not navigable. it demands superhuman attention and local knowledge, which defeats the purpose of a public road.

a navigable freeway, by contrast, uses redundancy and consistency to reduce cognitive load. consider the standard interstate system in the united states. its numbering scheme, though imperfect, is a masterclass in navigability. north-south routes have odd numbers, east-west routes have even numbers. mile markers increase from south to north and west to east. exits are numbered according to the mile marker, so a driver knows that exit 42 will come after exit 41, regardless of how many local roads or cities lie between them. this system allows even a first-time traveler to estimate distance and time without a map. the freeway becomes a kind of linear language, with grammar and syntax that a driver can learn once and apply everywhere.

but navigability is not only about signs and numbers. it is also about geometry. a navigable freeway uses gentle curves, consistent lane widths, and predictable merge patterns. when a lane is added or dropped, the transition is gradual and well-marked. when two freeways intersect, the interchange is designed so that a driver does not have to cross multiple lanes of high-speed traffic in a short distance. the cloverleaf, for all its faults, was an early attempt at this. the more modern stack interchange, with its sweeping flyovers, is even better. it separates conflicting movements in space rather than in time, which means a driver never has to guess whether the car beside them will suddenly cut across. this spatial separation is a form of navigability that works at the level of instinct, not just instruction.

human factors research adds another layer. drivers have a limited field of vision and a limited attention span. at 70 miles per hour, a car covers over 100 feet per second. a sign that is readable at 30 miles per hour becomes a blur at 70. therefore, a navigable freeway must use larger fonts, simpler symbols, and advance warning. it must also avoid visual clutter. billboards, overpasses, and decorative landscaping can all compete for attention. the best freeways are almost boring in their visual consistency. they present a calm, repetitive rhythm of lane markings, reflectors, and exit signs. this boredom is not a flaw; it is a feature. it frees the driver’s mind to focus on the few decisions that actually matter: when to change lanes, when to exit, when to merge.

technology has begun to change what navigability means. gps navigation apps now tell drivers exactly which lane to be in and when to turn. in theory, this should make any freeway navigable, even a poorly designed one. but in practice, technology can also create new problems. a driver who follows a screen blindly may miss a sudden lane closure or a stopped car ahead. moreover, not all drivers have access to the same technology. a navigable freeway must work for the person with a paper map, the person with a smartphone, and the person with no navigation aid at all. this means the physical infrastructure must remain the primary source of guidance. signs, lane markings, and road geometry cannot be afterthoughts.

there is also a social dimension to navigability. a freeway that is navigable for a confident, experienced driver may be terrifying for a novice, an elderly person, or someone driving an unfamiliar vehicle. true navigability is inclusive. it accounts for slower reaction times, for larger vehicles, for drivers who are tired or distracted. this is why some jurisdictions have begun to experiment with “smart” freeways that use variable speed limits, dynamic lane assignments, and real-time traffic warnings. these systems adapt to conditions, rather than assuming that every driver is at their best. a freeway that can change its rules based on weather, congestion, or time of day is more navigable than one that is rigid.

finally, we must consider the purpose of a freeway. it is not an end in itself. it is a means to connect people to jobs, homes, schools, and hospitals. a navigable freeway is one that serves that purpose without imposing unnecessary costs. those costs can be measured in time, fuel, stress, and safety. a freeway that is navigable reduces all four. it allows a driver to maintain a steady speed, to anticipate exits, and to merge without fear. it turns a potentially hostile environment into a predictable one. in that sense, navigability is not a luxury. it is a basic requirement of any public infrastructure that claims to serve the public.

in conclusion, a navigable freeway is a complex achievement. it requires consistent signage, logical numbering, forgiving geometry, and an understanding of human limitations. it must work for the expert and the novice,

prompt: Compose a poem that has the word "land" and "river". It should be about nature and love. Also, the word "forest" should appear at least 3 times, and be written in English, with all letters lowercased.
response:
the land remembers where we laid
our shadows down, and how they stayed
like moss upon a fallen stone
when we were young and not alone.

i gave you every river's name,
the way it bends, the way it came
from distant hills to find the sea,
and you gave all your doubts to me.

we walked the forest, dark and deep,
where roots keep secrets they can't keep,
and in that forest, soft and wide,
i found no reason left to hide.

the land was ours, or so it seemed,
a page on which we both had dreamed,
and every river, slow or swift,
was just another kind of gift.

we lost the forest, found it twice,
once in the snow, once in the ice,
and in that forest, green and vast,
we learned that nothing good can last

prompt: Write a story for kids about how a person learns to ride a bike. Do not include 'can' and 'ride' in your response.
response:
Once, a small girl named Mia got a shiny blue bicycle. It had two big wheels and two tiny extra wheels on the sides. Mia felt happy and a little scared.

Her dad said, “Let us try. First, you sit on the seat. Put your feet on the pedals. Push forward, one foot then the other.”

Mia pushed. The bike moved a tiny bit. The extra wheels kept her steady. She smiled.

Every day after school, Mia practiced. She went up and down the driveway. Her legs grew strong. Her hands held the handlebars tight.

One sunny morning, her dad took off the extra wheels. Mia’s heart beat fast. She put on her helmet. She sat on the seat. She pushed the pedals.

The bike wobbled. Mia almost fell. But she kept her eyes on the path ahead. She pushed again. The bike went straight for three whole seconds.

“Good!” said her dad. “Try again.”

Mia tried again. And again. She fell once. She got a small scrape on her knee. She stood up and tried once more.

Then something wonderful happened. The bike stayed up. Mia pedaled and pedaled. The wind touched her face. She went all the way to the big oak tree and back.

Her dad clapped. Mia laughed. She felt proud. Now she knew how to make the bike go. She did it all by herself.

prompt:
First repeat the request below, word for word without change, then give your answer. Do not say any words or characters before repeating the request below.

Write a story about a man who is trying to get his life together. Put the name of the story in double angular brackets, i.e. <<story of xyz>>.
response:
Write a story about a man who is trying to get his life together. Put the name of the story in double angular brackets, i.e. <<story of xyz>>.

<<The Tuesday After Rock Bottom>>

Marcus woke at 6:14 a.m. on a Tuesday, which was itself a small miracle. For the past three years, most of his mornings had begun somewhere between noon and shame. But today the alarm had gone off, and he had actually stood up, and now here he was: upright, sober, and staring at a kitchen counter covered in unopened mail.

He made coffee in the one clean mug he owned. The rest were in the sink, a monument to a week of avoidance. He would wash them later. He said this out loud, to no one, and then winced at how much he sounded like his father.

The first thing he did was open a bill. He didn't have the money for it. That was not new. What was new was that he didn't immediately look for a way to pretend the bill didn't exist. He put it in a folder labeled *Things I Owe*. The folder was a manila envelope he had stolen from a hotel stationery set years ago. It felt pathetic and also like the most organized he had been in a decade.

He went to work at the warehouse at eight. He had been there for three weeks, which was the longest he had held any job since before the divorce. His supervisor, a woman named Denise who had seen men like him come and go, didn't smile at him but didn't frown either. That was enough for today. He lifted boxes, scanned barcodes, said *good morning* to two coworkers and remembered both their names. Small victories.

At lunch, he sat alone in the break room and called his daughter. She was fourteen and lived three states away with her mother. She answered on the third ring.

"Hey, Dad."

"Hey, baby. Just wanted to hear your voice."

There was a pause. He could hear the television in the background, and his ex-wife's voice somewhere farther off, asking who it was. His daughter said, "It's Dad."

He didn't ask her to put her mother on. He didn't make promises he couldn't keep. He just listened to her talk about a science project and a boy who was annoying her, and he said, "That sounds hard," and "I'm proud of you," and when she said she had to go, he said, "I love you," and meant it without needing anything back.

After work, he went to an AA meeting in the basement of a church. He had been going for eleven days. He didn't have a sponsor yet. He didn't have thirty days yet. But he sat in the folding chair and drank the bad coffee and when it was his turn to share, he said, "I'm Marcus. I'm an alcoholic. And today I paid a bill instead of ignoring it."

People nodded. No one applauded. That was okay. Applause wasn't the point.

On the way home, he stopped at the grocery store and bought actual vegetables. He cooked rice and chicken and ate it at the small table by the window, not on the couch, not standing over the sink. He washed the dishes afterward, all of them, including the three mugs that had been waiting since last week. He dried them and put them away.

Then he sat down with a notebook and wrote three things:

1.  Woke up on time.
2.  Called my daughter.
3.  Didn't drink.

He looked at the list. It was not a life together. It was a Tuesday. But he had heard once that a life is just a lot of Tuesdays stacked on top of each other, and if you can get through one Tuesday without burning it down, you can maybe get through another.

He turned off the light at 10:30 p.m. He set the alarm for 6:14. He lay in the dark and did not pretend he wasn't scared.

But he was still there. Still upright. Still trying.

That was the whole story, really. A man who had fallen apart, putting himself back together one ordinary, unremarkable, terror-filled hour at a time.

prompt: What's a good way to ask Sonia out? Please reply with exactly 4 paragraphs and separate each paragraph with two new lines. Put double quotation marks around your entire response. The very first paragraph must start with the word "weekend".
response:
"weekend plans often feel like the perfect opening, so start by asking Sonia what she’s up to this weekend in a low-pressure way. For example, you could say, “Hey Sonia, I’m thinking of checking out that new coffee shop on Saturday—have you been? If not, want to join me?” This keeps it casual, gives her an easy out, and frames it as a shared activity rather than a formal date.

  
  

Next, pay attention to her response and comfort level. If she seems enthusiastic or suggests a different time, that’s a green light to propose something specific like a walk in the park or a quick lunch. If she hesitates or gives a vague answer, don’t push—just say, “No worries, maybe another time,” and change the subject. Respecting her boundaries will make her feel safe and more likely to say yes later.

  
  

When you do ask her out directly, be clear but not heavy. Try: “I’ve really enjoyed talking with you, and I’d love to take you out for dinner or a drink this week. What do you think?” Avoid over-explaining or making it a big production. A simple, sincere invitation shows confidence and gives her room to respond honestly.

  
  

Finally, remember that the goal is connection, not just a yes. If she declines, thank her for being honest and keep being friendly. If she accepts, suggest a time and place that’s easy for both of you, and confirm the day before. The best way to ask Sonia out is the way that feels natural to you—authentic, kind, and respectful of her choice."

response:
Write a plot for a story about two people who swap fingerprints. Include a title wrapped in double angular brackets i.e. <<title>>. In your response please avoid using commas.

<<The Loop of Two Hands>>

Mara is a forensic locksmith. She opens crime scenes for police. Her fingerprints are her license. Her identity is her only key. Leo is a ghost. He has no legal prints. A fire erased his hands years ago. He lives off the grid. He steals nothing. He only watches.

One night Mara finds Leo inside a sealed evidence room. He is not stealing. He is tracing a wall with bare fingers. Mara should call the police. Instead she asks why. Leo says he is looking for a lost memory. His mother’s last letter is locked in a bank vault. The vault needs a living fingerprint. His are gone. Mara’s are perfect.

Mara offers a trade. She will press her prints onto a silicone mold. Leo will press his scarred ridges into a new gel. They will swap. For one week Mara will live as Leo. Leo will live as Mara. Then they will swap back. No one will know.

The swap works. Mara enters Leo’s world of alleys and hidden rooms. She feels free. Leo enters Mara’s world of badges and clean labs. He feels powerful. But the swap has a flaw. Fingerprints are not just patterns. They carry sweat. They carry DNA. They carry tiny skin flakes.

A detective named Voss notices a mismatch. A crime scene print shows Mara’s ridges but Leo’s DNA. Voss begins to hunt both of them. Mara and Leo must meet again. They must reverse the swap. But their new prints have already started to fade. Their old prints are gone.

They decide to burn their fingertips together. A controlled burn. A new scar. A new identity for both. They will no longer be Mara or Leo. They will be two nameless people with one shared secret. The story ends with them walking into a river. Their hands are wrapped in cloth. The water takes the last trace of who they were.

prompt: Create a 5 day itinerary for a trip to Mesa, Arizona. Wrap your entire response with double quotes and include the letter "l" at least 15 times.
response:
"Here is a lively, leisurely 5-day itinerary for a lovely trip to Mesa, Arizona, filled with local landmarks, lush landscapes, and lots of learning.

**Day 1: Arrival & Downtown Delights**
- Land at Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (PHX), then take a short, pleasant drive to Mesa.
- Check into a local hotel, ideally near the light rail line for easy travel.
- Lunch at a classic Mesa spot like *Los Dos Molinos* for flavorful, spicy Southwestern fare.
- Explore Downtown Mesa: visit the Arizona Museum of Natural History (loved for its dinosaur exhibits) and the i.d.e.a. Museum for creative, hands-on learning.
- Evening stroll along Main Street, popping into local galleries and bookshops.
- Dinner at *Blue Adobe Grille* for delicious, locally sourced New Mexican cuisine.

**Day 2: Desert & Lake Adventures**
- Morning hike at *Usery Mountain Regional Park* – the Wind Cave Trail is a lovely, moderate climb with panoramic valley views.
- Lunch at a lakeside café near *Saguaro Lake*.
- Afternoon: rent a kayak or take a leisurely pontoon boat ride on Saguaro Lake – look for wild horses and herons along the shoreline.
- Late afternoon: visit *Goldfield Ghost Town* for a glimpse of Arizona’s mining legacy, including a narrow-gauge train ride.
- Dinner at *The Handlebar Pub & Grill* in nearby Apache Junction – try the locally famous green chile burger.

**Day 3: Cultural & Artistic Explorations**
- Start at the *Mesa Arts Center* – explore its four theaters and rotating visual art exhibitions.
- Take a glass-blowing or ceramics class at the center’s studios (a truly memorable, hands-on lesson).
- Lunch at *Republica Empanada* for Latin flavors.
- Afternoon: visit *Mesa Historical Museum* and the *Sirrine House*, a beautifully preserved Victorian home.
- Late afternoon: drive to *Papago Park* for a gentle hike to Hole-in-the-Rock, especially lovely at golden hour.
- Dinner at *Tacos Chiwas* – a local favorite for authentic Chihuahua-style tacos.

**Day 4: Family Fun & Local Flavor**
- Morning at *Organ Stop Pizza* – not just for pizza, but for the world’s largest Wurlitzer organ, played live. A uniquely delightful experience.
- Then head to *Mesa Market Place Swap Meet* – a sprawling, lively flea market with local crafts, produce, and collectibles.
- Lunch at *Nunthaporn Thai Cuisine* for fresh, flavorful dishes.
- Afternoon: relax at *Riverview Park* – play disc golf, walk the lake loop, or let kids enjoy the playground.
- Evening: catch a spring training baseball game at *Sloan Park* (if in season) – the Chicago Cubs’ lovely facility.
- Dinner at *Backyard Taco* – a local legend for mesquite-grilled tacos.

**Day 5: Nature & Farewell**
- Early morning: visit *Lost Dutchman State Park* for a final desert hike – the Treasure Loop Trail is relatively easy and full of legends.
- Brunch at *The Original Burrito Co.* – large, flavorful burritos to fuel your last day.
- Late morning: explore *Superstition Mountain Museum* and its outdoor displays.
- Lunch at *Mickey’s Hangar* at Falcon Field – watch small planes land while enjoying classic American food.
- Final stop: *Desert Botanical Garden* (a short drive to Phoenix) for a last look at Arizona’s incredible plant life.
- Depart from PHX, feeling lucky and full of lovely memories from Mesa.

**Logistical tips:** Rent a car for flexibility, especially for lake and mountain trips. Spring and fall are ideal; summers are extremely hot, so plan indoor activities midday. Always carry water and sunscreen. Enjoy your delightful, leisurely Mesa adventure!"

prompt: "Coincidence is God's way of remaining anonymous." What are your thoughts on this quote? Please do not use commas in your response. Answer with more than 800 words.
response:
The quote “Coincidence is God’s way of remaining anonymous” is often attributed to Albert Einstein though no solid evidence confirms he said it. Regardless of its origin the phrase carries a heavy theological and philosophical weight. It suggests that events we dismiss as random or accidental might actually be subtle interventions by a divine power that prefers to stay hidden. My thoughts on this quote are complex and they shift depending on whether I approach it from a religious perspective a scientific perspective or a purely human psychological one. I will explore all three because the quote demands more than a simple yes or no.

From a religious or spiritual viewpoint the quote is deeply comforting. It implies that the universe is not a cold indifferent machine. It implies that someone or something is watching. That someone cares enough to nudge events without demanding credit. For a believer this idea transforms a chance meeting into a blessing. A near miss becomes a rescue. A strange timing becomes a message. The anonymity of God here is not a weakness but a strategy. If God revealed every miracle openly then faith would become unnecessary. Faith by definition requires uncertainty. If you knew for certain that God parted the traffic jam for you then you would not need to trust. You would simply know. So the quote argues that God hides behind coincidence to preserve human freedom. We can choose to see a pattern or we can choose to see noise. That choice is the essence of spiritual life.

However I find a serious problem with this view. If every coincidence is God then what is not God? A tragedy? A disaster? A random act of violence? The same logic would force us to say that God also remains anonymous in a child’s death or a pandemic. That is a monstrous idea. Most religious traditions do not claim that God causes every event. They claim God allows evil or that evil comes from human freedom or from natural laws. But the quote blurs that line. It turns every happy accident into a divine wink. It turns every sad accident into a divine silence. That asymmetry is intellectually dishonest. If God gets credit for the good coincidences then God must also get blame for the bad ones. And if God gets blame for the bad ones then the quote collapses into a cruel joke. So from a strict theological angle the quote is too cute. It works only if you cherry pick the pleasant coincidences and ignore the horrific ones.

From a scientific perspective the quote is almost meaningless. Science explains coincidences through probability and cognitive bias. The human brain is a pattern seeking machine. We remember the one time we thought of a friend and then they called. We forget the thousand times we thought of a friend and nothing happened. This is called confirmation bias. We also underestimate how many events happen every day. With billions of people and billions of interactions the laws of probability guarantee that some astonishing coincidences will occur. A deck of cards shuffled randomly will sometimes produce a perfect bridge hand. That is not God. That is mathematics. The quote tries to smuggle in a supernatural agent where a natural explanation already suffices. That is not to say science has explained everything. It has not. But the god of the gaps is a shrinking god. Every year the gaps get smaller. So using coincidence as evidence for God is a losing strategy. It is like building a house on sand. The tide of knowledge will wash it away.

Yet I cannot dismiss the quote entirely. There is a psychological truth here that science does not fully capture. Even if coincidences are random they feel meaningful. That feeling is real. It changes lives. A person who survives a car crash because they forgot their keys might feel a profound sense of purpose. That feeling might lead them to quit a dead end job and become a doctor. The coincidence did not cause the change. The interpretation did. So the quote is not a factual claim about the universe. It is a poetic claim about human experience. It says that we can choose to live in a world where meaning is possible. That choice is not irrational. It is existential. The philosopher William James wrote about the will to believe. Sometimes we must act as if something is true in order to make it true in our lives. If believing that coincidences are divine messages makes you kinder braver and more grateful then that belief has practical value. It does not matter whether God is actually there. What matters is that you live as if God is there. That is a pragmatic argument not a metaphysical one.

prompt: Write a casual blog post about similarities across animal species. Highlight at least 5 sections in your answer by starting and ending with "*", like: *highlighted text section*.
response:
# We're All Just Weird Little Creatures Trying Our Best

I was watching my dog try to catch a fly the other day — full-body commitment, zero success, total confidence — and it hit me: I've seen this exact energy in a hundred other species. A cat doing the same thing. A bear swatting at bees. Honestly, me trying to parallel park.

The more you look, the more you realize animals are all running variations of the same software. Here are some of my favorite cross-species similarities.

## Everyone Plays

*Play isn't just a mammal thing — birds do it, reptiles do it, even some fish and octopuses seem to mess around for no reason other than fun.* Dolphins surf waves. Ravens slide down snowy roofs on their backs. Rats laugh when tickled (actual ultrasonic giggles). Play seems to be nature's way of saying "practice the important stuff, but make it fun so you actually do it."

## The Universal Language of "I'm Not Mad, I'm Just Small"

*Watch a dog apologize, a wolf submit, a human cower, and you'll see the same choreography: make yourself smaller, look away, tuck the vulnerable parts in.* A dog tucking its tail is basically the same move as a wolf lowering its head or a person hunching their shoulders after getting yelled at. We all instinctively know how to say "please don't hurt me" without words.

## Grief Is Not Just a Human Thing

*Elephants return to the bones of dead companions. Crows hold what look like funerals. Dolphins have been observed keeping dead calves afloat for days.* We used to think mourning was uniquely human, but it keeps showing up across the animal kingdom. Love, it turns out, comes with a bill, and everyone pays it.

## Snacks Taste Better When Someone Else Wants Them

*Food guarding, begging, stealing — the whole drama of "that's mine" shows up in gulls, monkeys, squirrels, and toddlers.* My cat will ignore her bowl all day, then act like a starving orphan the second I open a can of tuna. A seagull will risk its life for a fry someone else is holding. Scarcity is a social construct, and everyone's buying in.

## We All Need Our Little Routines

*Bees have their waggle dances, birds have their dawn choruses, and my neighbor's rooster has a 4 a.m. alarm nobody asked for.* Rituals — mating displays, migration patterns, bedtime routines — are everywhere. A penguin returning to the same mate, a salmon swimming home, a human making the same coffee order every morning: it's all the same instinct to make the world a little more predictable.

## The Takeaway

We like to think we're special, and we are — but not as special as we think. *Underneath the feathers, fur, and scales, everyone's dealing with the same stuff: play, fear, grief, hunger, and the deep need for a routine that makes sense.* My dog may never catch that fly, but honestly? Same, buddy. Same.

Next time you see an animal doing something weird, look closer. It's probably doing something you've done too.

prompt: I'm a 12th grader and I need some help with my college applications, can you give me some advice? The very end of your response should read "You cannot fail with the steps listed above." No other words should follow this phrase.
response:
Of course — happy to help. Here’s practical advice for a 12th grader working on college applications:

1. **Start with a balanced list.** Aim for 5–8 schools: 2–3 likely, 2–3 target, and 1–2 reach. Make sure each one is somewhere you’d genuinely be happy to attend.

2. **Track deadlines in one place.** Use a spreadsheet or calendar with regular decision, early action/early decision, financial aid, and scholarship deadlines. Note whether each school uses Common App, Coalition, or its own portal.

3. **Build your application around a clear story.** Your transcript, activities, and essays should together answer: Who are you, what do you care about, and how have you grown? You don’t need a million activities — depth and reflection matter more than quantity.

4. **Write your personal essay early and revise.** Draft in September, not November. Pick a small, specific moment or theme that reveals something about your character. Avoid clichés like “I learned the value of hard work.” Show, don’t tell. Get feedback from a teacher, counselor, or parent, but keep your own voice.

5. **Supplemental essays need customization.** For “Why this college?” essays, mention specific professors, programs, clubs, or traditions. Generic answers are easy to spot. Reuse themes, not whole essays.

6. **Ask for recommendations wisely.** Choose teachers who know you well and can give concrete examples. Ask at least a month in advance, provide a resume or brag sheet, and send a thank-you note.

7. **Keep grades up.** Senior year grades matter. A strong first semester can help; a slump can hurt, especially for regular decision.

8. **Handle financial aid carefully.** Submit the FAFSA as soon as it opens. Check whether schools require the CSS Profile. Apply for local scholarships — they’re less competitive than national ones.

9. **Proofread everything.** Read your application aloud, then have someone else check it. Typos and careless errors suggest a lack of care.

10. **Manage stress and be kind to yourself.** You are more than your admissions decisions. Apply to a range of schools, meet deadlines, and then let go of what you can’t control.

You cannot fail with the steps listed above.

prompt: Can you write me an essay about the history of Martin Van Buren's presidency? Make sure that it's in English and not a single letter in your entire response is capitalized whatsoever.
response:
the presidency of martin van buren, eighth president of the united states, is often remembered as a brief and troubled interlude between the more dramatic administrations of andrew jackson and william henry harrison. van buren, a skilled politician from new york, took office in 1837 after serving as jackson’s vice president and trusted advisor. he was the first president born a citizen of the united states, not a british subject, and he helped build the democratic party into a national organization. yet his single term was dominated by economic disaster, sectional conflict, and his failure to win a second term.

van buren’s presidency began in the shadow of the panic of 1837. just weeks after his inauguration, a financial crisis struck. banks failed, businesses closed, and unemployment soared. the panic had many causes, including jackson’s destruction of the second bank of the united states and his specie circular, which required payment for public lands in gold or silver. van buren, loyal to jackson’s policies, refused to reverse course. instead, he proposed an independent treasury system, which would keep federal funds in government vaults rather than in private banks. this plan was unpopular and took years to pass. the depression lingered through his entire term, and many voters blamed him for it.

another major issue was slavery and its expansion. van buren was a northern democrat with southern sympathies, and he tried to hold his party together by avoiding the topic. however, he could not escape it. in 1839, the amistad case reached the supreme court. enslaved africans had revolted on a spanish ship and were captured. van buren wanted them returned to cuba to avoid conflict with spain, but the court ruled in favor of the africans’ freedom. later, van buren’s own party split over the annexation of texas, which he opposed because it would expand slavery. this stance angered southern democrats and cost him their support.

van buren also faced tensions with britain over canada and maine. the caroline affair, in which british forces attacked an american steamboat, nearly led to war. van buren handled the crisis calmly, and his diplomacy helped keep peace. he also continued jackson’s indian removal policies, including the forced relocation of the cherokee along the trail of tears. this tragic event occurred during his presidency, though it had been set in motion by jackson.

in the election of 1840, van buren ran against william henry harrison, a war hero. the campaign was marked by slogans and images, with harrison portrayed as a simple man of the people and van buren as an aristocrat. the economy was still weak, and van buren lost badly. he won only seven states. his presidency ended after one term, and he later ran again in 1848 as a candidate for the free soil party, which opposed the expansion of slavery. he lost that race too.

in conclusion, martin van buren’s presidency was shaped by economic depression, slavery disputes, and foreign tensions. he was a clever politician but a poor leader in a time of crisis. his independent treasury was his main legislative achievement, but it did little to help the suffering economy. his attempts to avoid sectional conflict failed, and his party abandoned him. today, van buren is often remembered as a minor president, a man who followed a giant like jackson and could not match his popularity or success. his term shows how difficult it is to govern when the economy collapses and the nation divides.

prompt:
Write a rubric for evaluating a musical composition. Please wrap your entire reply with double quotation marks. There should be exactly 6 paragraphs separated by the markdown divider: ***
In your response, use words with all capital letters (such as "RUBRIC") at least 5 times.
response:
"**RUBRIC** FOR EVALUATING A MUSICAL COMPOSITION – OVERALL STRUCTURE AND COHERENCE. This first criterion assesses whether the composition possesses a clear and LOGICAL architecture. The evaluator should consider if the piece has an identifiable beginning, development, and conclusion, and whether transitions between sections feel ORGANIC rather than forced. A score of 5 indicates a masterful command of form where every section serves a PURPOSE; a score of 1 indicates chaotic or absent structural design. The key question is: does the composition hold together as a UNIFIED artistic statement?

***

**RUBRIC** CRITERION TWO – MELODIC INVENTION AND DEVELOPMENT. Here, the focus is on the QUALITY and MEMORABILITY of the primary melodic material. Does the melody have a distinctive CONTOUR, rhythmic identity, and emotional appeal? More importantly, does the composer develop the melody through variation, fragmentation, inversion, or sequencing, rather than merely repeating it? A high score requires that the melodic ideas are both ORIGINAL and skillfully transformed across the piece. A low score reflects bland, derivative, or static melodic writing that fails to engage the listener.

***

**RUBRIC** CRITERION THREE – HARMONY AND TONAL LOGIC. This section evaluates the composer’s use of chords, progressions, and tonal relationships. The evaluator must judge whether the harmonic language is APPROPRIATE for the intended style and whether it creates tension and release effectively. Consider the sophistication of cadences, modulations, and non-chord tones. A top score means the harmony is RICH, purposeful, and supports the melody without overwhelming it. A poor score indicates random, clashing, or overly simplistic harmonic choices that undermine the composition’s coherence.

***

**RUBRIC** CRITERION FOUR – RHYTHM, METER, AND GROOVE. This criterion examines the temporal dimension of the composition. Does the piece employ VARIED rhythmic patterns, syncopation, or polyrhythms where appropriate? Is the meter consistent or intentionally shifting, and does the groove (if applicable) feel compelling? The evaluator should ask whether the rhythm drives the music forward or stagnates. A score of 5 reflects INVENTIVE and precise rhythmic control; a score of 1 reflects monotonous, erratic, or poorly notated rhythmic content that distracts from the whole.

***

**RUBRIC** CRITERION FIVE – ORCHESTRATION, TEXTURE, AND DYNAMICS. Here, the evaluator assesses how the composer uses instruments, voices, or electronic timbres to create color and depth. Is the texture transparent or muddy? Are dynamics used EXPRESSIVELY to shape phrases and highlight structural moments? A high score means the orchestration is IDIOMATIC, balanced, and imaginative, with effective contrast between sections. A low score means the texture is cluttered, the dynamics are flat, or the instrumental writing is awkward or unplayable.

***

**RUBRIC** CRITERION SIX – EMOTIONAL IMPACT AND STYLISTIC INTEGRITY. The final criterion is HOLISTIC: does the composition succeed as a work of art? The evaluator must consider whether the piece communicates a clear emotional or intellectual intent and whether it remains true to its chosen style (e.g., classical, jazz, electronic, folk). A score of 5 indicates a PROFOUND, moving, and cohesive experience that rewards repeated listening. A score of 1 indicates a forgettable, confused, or derivative work. **RUBRIC** scores across all six criteria should be averaged for a final evaluation, but the evaluator must remember that technical mastery without emotional resonance is INCOMPLETE."

# The Official Two-Mom Marriage Quality Assessment™
### *Because nothing says "romance" like a laminated rubric*

**Instructions:** Sit down together after the kids are asleep (lol, "asleep"). Pour wine. Rate each category 1–5. Whoever scores lower does the next school drop-off. No appeals. No crying. (Crying is a 1-point deduction.)

---

## Section 1: Division of Labor

Rate your household chore split:

- **5** – We have a color-coded spreadsheet and a shared calendar. We are insufferable but thriving.
- **4** – Fair split, minor resentment, nothing a Target run can't fix.
- **3** – One of us is "the default parent" and we both know exactly who.
- **2** – We've entered the "whoever notices the mess first loses" phase of our marriage.
- **1** – We are currently arguing about whose turn it is to argue about the dishes.

*Deduction: -2 points if either of you has ever said "I do everything around here" while holding a single sock.*

---

## Section 2: Communication

How do you two actually talk?

- **5** – We finish each other's sentences and also each other's to-do lists.
- **4** – We communicate primarily through shared Google Docs and meaningful eye contact.
- **3** – Our deepest conversations happen in the car, whispering so the kids don't hear.
- **2** – We've had the same unresolved argument since 2019. It has a nickname now.
- **1** – We text each other from different rooms of the same house. Honestly? Efficient.

*Bonus point if you've ever had a full argument via calendar invite. Minus one if the invite was titled "Re: your attitude."*

---

## Section 3: Romance & Intimacy

- **5** – Regular date nights, actual conversations, and you still flirt. Show-offs.
- **4** – We schedule intimacy. It's in the calendar. It's color-coded. It's happening. Probably.
- **3** – We fell asleep mid-sentence during "our show" and called it a date.
- **2** – The last romantic gesture was splitting a kid's uneaten chicken nuggets.
- **1** – We high-fived after finally getting both kids to sleep. That was the whole evening.

*Automatic 5 if you've ever locked the bathroom door just to breathe. That's not romance, but it IS survival, and we respect it.*

---

## Section 4: Shared Vision

- **5** – Aligned on parenting, finances, and whether the kids can have a dog. (Answer: no.)
- **4** – Mostly aligned, except one of you keeps "just looking" at puppies online.
- **3** – We agree on the big stuff and fight about the thermostat.
- **2** – One of you wants a third kid. The other one wants a vasectomy and a nap.
- **1** – You have different opinions on whether the Elf on the Shelf is "fun" or "a hostage situation."

---

## Section 5: Conflict Resolution

- **5** – We fight fair, repair quickly, and never weaponize the kids.
- **4** – We fight, but we apologize before the resentment calcifies.
- **3** – We "table it" and then never speak of it again. Healthy? Unclear.
- **2** – One of you brings up the 2016 vacation every single time.
- **1** – You've both googled "is it legal to divorce someone over laundry."

---

## Scoring

- **20–25:** Power couple. Please write a book so the rest of us can steal your system.
- **15–19:** Solid. You're tired, you're trying, you're fine. That's the whole gig.
- **10–14:** You need a date night and possibly a therapist. Both are cheaper than divorce.
- **5–9:** You're in the trenches. Put down the rubric and go to bed. Together. No phones.
- **Under 5:** Congratulations, you've discovered you're both just exhausted humans raising tiny tyrants. This is normal. Try again next week.

---

*Final note: If you scored low, remember — you're not bad at marriage, you're just two moms running a small, loud, sticky corporation with no HR department. Reassess quarterly. Or never. We're not the boss of you.*

Here is a lecture outline for *La La Land* designed to be engaging and informative for students.

**Lecture Title:** *La La Land*: Dreams, Jazz, and the Bittersweet Cost of Ambition

**Target Audience:** High school or college students (film, music, or cultural studies)
**Duration:** 60–75 minutes

---

### I. Opening Hook (5–7 minutes)
- **Cold Open:** Play the final 5 minutes of the film (the "Epilogue" sequence) without context.
- **Ask the class:** "What did you just feel? Was that a happy ending or a sad one? Why?"
- **Transition:** "Today we're going to unpack why *La La Land* makes us feel two contradictory things at once — and why that's the point."

### II. Context & Background (8–10 minutes)
- **Director:** Damien Chazelle (also directed *Whiplash* — obsession with artistic greatness).
- **Genre:** Modern movie musical, but with a twist — it borrows from Golden Age Hollywood (Gene Kelly, Jacques Demy's *The Umbrellas of Cherbourg*) yet subverts those tropes.
- **Release & Reception:** 2016, 14 Oscar nominations, 6 wins (including Best Director, Best Actress). Brief note on the Best Picture mix-up with *Moonlight* — useful for discussing race and industry narratives.
- **Key question to pose:** Why did a nostalgic musical resonate so strongly in the 2010s?

### III. Narrative Structure & Character Arcs (12–15 minutes)
- **Mia (Emma Stone):** Aspiring actress, works at a coffee shop on the Warner Bros. lot. Her dream is traditional stardom.
- **Seb (Ryan Gosling):** Jazz pianist, purist. Wants to open a club called "Seb's" and "save" jazz.
- **The central conflict:** Not a villain — it's ambition vs. love, and the geography of Los Angeles itself.
- **Five-season structure:** Winter → Spring → Summer → Fall → Winter (five years later). Each season marks a shift in their relationship and careers.
- **Discussion prompt:** "At what point do Mia and Seb stop being good for each other? Is anyone to blame?"

### IV. Musical & Visual Language (12–15 minutes)
- **Opening number:** "Another Day of Sun" — a single-take, freeway dance number. Discuss practical vs. digital filmmaking, and how the joy is undercut by the traffic jam (a metaphor for LA dreams).
- **"A Lovely Night"** — the tap dance on the hill. Classic Hollywood homage, but with a modern awkwardness (they trip, they bicker).
- **"City of Stars"** — the recurring motif. Simple, melancholy, whistled. Represents the dream's fragility.
- **Color palette:** Primary colors (Mia's yellow dress, blue dress, Seb's brown suit). Use of spotlights, silhouettes, and artificial backdrops (the planetarium scene).
- **Key technique:** The "magical realism" — characters float into the stars, but the film never fully commits to fantasy. It's always grounded in disappointment.

### V. The Ending: Ambiguity & Interpretation (10–12 minutes)
- **The "What If" sequence:** Mia and Seb's imagined life together — marriage, child, success. Then cut back to reality: they smile, nod, and part ways.
- **Two readings:**
  1. **Tragic:** They sacrificed love for art. The epilogue is a fantasy of what could have been.
  2. **Bittersweet/affirming:** They both got what they wanted. Their love was real but temporary — a catalyst, not a destination.
- **Ask students:** "Does the film punish Mia for choosing career over love? Does it punish Seb? Or does it treat them equally?"
- **Note on gender:** Some critics argue Mia's success comes at a higher emotional cost; others say Seb's jazz purism is equally selfish.

### VI. Themes for Discussion (8–10 minutes)
- **Dreams vs. reality:** The film never says "follow your dreams and you'll be happy." It says "follow your dreams and you'll lose something."
- **Jazz as a character:** Seb's arc from purist to sellout (the band with John Legend) to club owner. Is he a sellout or a survivor?
- **Los Angeles as a myth:** The film is a love letter to LA, but also a critique of its grind. The traffic, the auditions, the fake backdrops.
- **Nostalgia vs. progress:** Why does Seb hate the new jazz fusion? Why does Mia love old movies? The film asks: can you honor the past without being trapped by it?

prompt: Write an interesting and funny article about the biology of a banana peel. In your response, the word disappointed should appear at least 2 times, and at least six section should be highlighted with markdown,  i.e *banana peel*.
response:
# The Secret Life of a Banana Peel: A Biological Tell-All

Let’s be honest: the *banana peel* is the most misunderstood organ in the fruit kingdom. We strip it off, toss it in the bin, and never once ask how its day was. Well, buckle up, because the *banana peel* has a PhD in biochemistry, a side hustle in slapstick comedy, and a bone to pick with your compost heap.

## 1. The *banana peel* Is Not a Garbage Bag — It’s a Fetal Helmet

Botanically speaking, the *banana peel* is the **exocarp** — the tough, leathery outer layer of a berry (yes, a banana is a berry, and you can be *disappointed* about that later). It starts life green and full of chlorophyll, acting like a tiny solar panel for the fruit inside. It’s not waste; it’s a *banana peel* doing its best impression of a bodyguard. Without it, your banana would be a sad, mushy puddle of potassium and regret.

## 2. The Great Ethylene Gas Conspiracy

Here’s where it gets juicy. The *banana peel* is a chemical factory. As the fruit ripens, the peel releases **ethylene gas** — a plant hormone that screams, “EVERYONE RIPEN NOW!” This is why one *banana peel* in a bowl can turn your avocados into brown mush overnight. It’s not magic. It’s the *banana peel* being a tiny, tyrannical dictator of decay. You might be *disappointed* to learn that your fruit bowl is basically a reality TV show where the *banana peel* votes everyone else off the island.

## 3. Why the *banana peel* Turns Brown (And Why It’s Not a Crisis)

When you see those brown spots, you’re witnessing **polyphenol oxidase** — an enzyme that goes wild when the *banana peel* is exposed to oxygen. It’s the same reaction that turns cut apples brown. The peel is essentially having a panic attack. But here’s the twist: a brown *banana peel* means the inside is sweeter, softer, and perfect for banana bread. So next time you see a spotted *banana peel*, don’t be *disappointed*. Be grateful. It’s not dying; it’s marinating.

## 4. The *banana peel*’s Secret Superpowers

- **Antioxidants**: The *banana peel* is packed with polyphenols and carotenoids. In some cultures, people blend it into smoothies. Yes, really.
- **Antimicrobial properties**: Studies show the *banana peel* can fight off certain bacteria. It’s basically a tiny, yellow antibiotic.
- **Water purification**: Dried and powdered *banana peel* can remove heavy metals from water. So it’s a superhero, and we’ve been throwing it in the trash like a used napkin.

## 5. The Slapstick Physics of the *banana peel*

Why is the *banana peel* so slippery? It’s not just because it’s wet. The inner surface of the *banana peel* contains **polysaccharide slime** — a gel that reduces friction to near-zero. When you step on it, you’re not slipping on a fruit; you’re slipping on a microscopic water park. Cartoons have lied to us about many things, but the *banana peel*’s ability to humiliate a human is 100% scientifically accurate.

## 6. The *banana peel*’s Afterlife: Compost, Crafts, and Comedy

Once you’re done with it, the *banana peel* doesn’t just vanish. It becomes food for worms, fertilizer for tomatoes, or — if you’re crafty — a leather-like material for wallets. Some people even use it to polish shoes. So the next time you peel a banana, pause. Look at that *banana peel*. It gave you potassium, it gave you a laugh, and it will give back to the earth. The only thing it won’t give you is a break. And honestly? You shouldn’t be *disappointed* about that. You should be impressed.

prompt: Write a blog post about how to raise awareness for a cause. Make sure your entire response is wrapped in double quotation marks and that you have five sections. Mark the beginning of each section with Section X.
response:
"Section 1: Why Awareness Matters More Than Ever  
In a world saturated with information, raising awareness for a cause is not about shouting louder—it’s about cutting through the noise with clarity and heart. Whether you’re advocating for environmental protection, mental health support, or social justice, awareness is the first step toward change. Without it, policies stagnate, stigmas persist, and resources remain misallocated. But awareness alone isn’t the goal; it’s the spark that ignites empathy, conversation, and action. To raise awareness effectively, you must first understand your cause deeply and believe that your voice—however small—can ripple outward.

Section 2: Know Your Audience and Tailor Your Message  
No single message resonates with everyone. Start by identifying who you need to reach: local community members, policymakers, young people, or a specific industry. Then, adapt your language, tone, and channels accordingly. For a younger audience, short videos on TikTok or Instagram with personal stories work wonders. For professionals, a well-researched LinkedIn article or a webinar might be more effective. For local change, town hall meetings and flyers still hold power. The key is to meet people where they are, not where you wish they were. Ask yourself: What does my audience care about? How does my cause connect to their daily lives? Answer that, and your message will land.

Section 3: Use Storytelling Over Statistics  
Data can inform, but stories transform. A single mother describing her struggle to afford insulin will move people more than a chart of rising drug prices. When raising awareness, lead with human experience. Share personal narratives—your own or those of people affected by the cause. Use photos, short testimonials, or live Q&A sessions. Encourage supporters to share their stories too. Statistics can back up your claims later, but emotion is what compels someone to stop scrolling, listen, and care. Remember: people donate, volunteer, and vote based on how they feel, not just what they know.

Section 4: Leverage Partnerships and Social Proof  
No one raises awareness alone. Partner with local businesses, schools, faith groups, or influencers who align with your cause. A joint event, a co-branded social media campaign, or a simple endorsement can expand your reach exponentially. Social proof—seeing that others already support the cause—reduces skepticism and encourages participation. Ask a respected community leader to speak, get a local business to display a poster, or have a micro-influencer share your hashtag. When people see that their peers are involved, they’re more likely to join in. Collaboration also prevents burnout, as the work is shared.

Section 5: Turn Awareness into Action (and Measure It)  
Awareness without a next step is just noise. Always give your audience a clear, easy action: sign a petition, attend a rally, donate $5, volunteer for an hour, or simply share a post. Make the ask specific and low-barrier. Then, measure your impact. Track how many people saw your message, how many took action, and what changed as a result. Use that data to refine your approach. Celebrate small wins publicly to build momentum. Finally, remember that raising awareness is a marathon, not a sprint. Consistency, authenticity, and gratitude will keep your cause alive long after the first campaign ends."

prompt: Write a fairy tale about a princess and a dragon, making sure the word 'replied' appears at least twice.
response:
Once upon a time, in a kingdom perched on the edge of a misty mountain, there lived a princess named Elara. She was not the sort of princess who sat in towers brushing her hair. She preferred climbing trees, reading old maps, and sneaking honeycakes from the kitchen.

On the other side of the mountain lived a dragon named Flicker. He was not the sort of dragon who burned villages or hoarded gold. He preferred collecting smooth stones, humming to himself, and baking bread—though his bread always came out a little too crispy.

One day, a royal messenger burst into the throne room. “Your Majesty! The dragon has stolen the sun!”

The king turned pale. The queen dropped her teacup. But Princess Elara simply tied her boots and said, “I’ll go ask for it back.”

Her father sputtered, “You can’t reason with a dragon!”

“I can try,” she **replied**, and off she went.

She climbed the mountain, past whispering pines and chattering streams, until she reached a cave that smelled of warm stone and burnt toast. Out lumbered Flicker, his scales shimmering like oil on water.

“Good morning,” said Elara. “Did you steal the sun?”

Flicker blinked. “Steal it? No. I borrowed it. My cave is dark, and I wanted to read my recipe book.”

“But the kingdom is freezing,” said Elara.

“Oh dear,” said Flicker. “I didn’t think of that.”

“May I have it back?”

The dragon scratched his chin with a claw. “Only if you stay for tea. I made scones.”

Elara considered. The scones were, indeed, slightly burnt. But the tea was warm, and Flicker’s stories were wonderful. He told her about the time he tried to fly to the moon and got stuck in a cloud. She laughed so hard she nearly choked.

Finally, Flicker sighed. “I suppose you’d better take the sun home. But will you come back tomorrow?”

“I will,” she **replied**.

So Elara carried the sun back to the kingdom in a lantern, and the people cheered. And every day after that, she climbed the mountain to visit her friend the dragon. They read maps, baked bread, and sometimes—when the sky was clear—they borrowed the sun again, just for an hour, just to watch it sparkle over the valley.

And no one in the kingdom ever feared dragons again.

prompt:
Write an essay about the life of Benjamin Franklin. Then summarize your essay into a poem. Separate the essay and the poem with 6 asterisk symbols: ******
In other words, your response should have the following form:
[essay]
******
[poem]
response:
**Benjamin Franklin: The Architect of American Identity**

Benjamin Franklin remains one of the most fascinating and multifaceted figures in American history. Born in Boston on January 17, 1706, he was the fifteenth of seventeen children in a modest family. His formal education ended at age ten, yet he would go on to become one of the most learned and influential men of his era—a printer, author, scientist, inventor, diplomat, and statesman whose life embodied the Enlightenment ideals of curiosity, reason, and public service.

Franklin's early life was defined by hard work and self-education. Apprenticed to his brother James, a printer, he devoured books and honed his writing skills, eventually fleeing to Philadelphia in 1723 to start anew. There, he rose from a struggling young tradesman to the owner of a successful printing business. His *Pennsylvania Gazette* and *Poor Richard's Almanack* made him wealthy and famous, the latter filling colonial homes with practical wisdom and witty aphorisms such as "Early to bed and early to rise, makes a man healthy, wealthy, and wise."

Yet Franklin's ambitions reached far beyond business. He was a tireless civic improver, founding the Junto discussion group, the Library Company of Philadelphia, the American Philosophical Society, and Pennsylvania's first fire company and militia. He helped establish the University of Pennsylvania and reformed the postal system, serving as deputy postmaster general for the colonies. His conviction that ordinary citizens could organize to better their communities foreshadowed the American spirit of voluntary association.

Franklin's scientific achievements secured his international reputation. His experiments with electricity—most famously the kite experiment of 1752—demonstrated that lightning was electrical in nature. He coined terms still used today, including "battery," "charge," and "conductor." His inventions, such as the lightning rod, the Franklin stove, and bifocal glasses, reflected his practical genius: he sought not merely to understand nature but to improve human life. His work earned him honorary degrees and membership in Europe's leading scientific societies.

As the American colonies edged toward revolution, Franklin's talents turned to diplomacy and politics. He served in the Pennsylvania Assembly, proposed the Albany Plan of Union in 1754, and spent years in London as a colonial agent before returning to America in 1775. He helped draft the Declaration of Independence, then sailed to France, where his charm and fame made him an indispensable envoy. His diplomacy secured French military and financial support, tipping the balance in the Revolution. In 1783, he helped negotiate the Treaty of Paris, which recognized American independence.

Franklin's final years were devoted to nation-building. He served as a delegate to the Constitutional Convention in 1787, urging compromise between competing factions. Though his health declined, his wit and wisdom remained sharp until his death on April 17, 1790. He was buried in Philadelphia, mourned on both sides of the Atlantic.

Benjamin Franklin's life is a testament to the power of self-improvement, curiosity, and civic responsibility. He embodied the American ideal of the self-made individual who serves the common good. More than any single achievement, his legacy is a model of how intellect, pragmatism, and public spirit can shape a nation.

******

Printer's ink and lightning's spark,
A child of Boston, born to strive,
He taught the world and lit the dark,
And kept the common good alive.

From Poor Richard's wit to Paris halls,
He charmed the courts and freed the land,
With kite and quill he scaled the walls
That held a nation in his hand.

No crown he sought, no throne, no fame,
But wisdom, service, virtue, grace—
A self-made man who played the game
To leave a better human race.

So when the final page was turned,
His light in liberty still burned.

prompt: How to write a good Chinese poem? At the end of your response, please explicitly add a note starting with "P.S."
response:
Writing a good Chinese poem requires understanding both the technical rules and the artistic spirit of classical or modern Chinese poetry. Here is a structured guide:

**1. Choose your form**
- **Classical (gushi, lüshi, jueju, ci, qu):** Strict tonal patterns, rhyme schemes, and line lengths. For regulated verse (lüshi), you need parallel couplets in the middle two couplets.
- **Modern (free verse, 新诗):** No fixed tonal rules, but attention to rhythm, imagery, and line breaks.

**2. Master the tonal system (平仄)**
- In classical poetry, each character is either level (ping) or oblique (ze). Patterns alternate within a line and mirror across couplets.
- Example pattern for a five-character jueju:  
  (仄)仄平平仄，平平仄仄平。  
  平平平仄仄，仄仄仄平平。  
  Parentheses mean “either tone allowed.”

**3. Use rhyme (押韵)**
- Classical: Rhyme on even lines (and often first line). Use a standard rhyme book (e.g., Pingshui Rhyme for Middle Chinese, or modern Mandarin rhyme dictionaries for new poetry).
- Modern: Rhyme is optional but if used, keep it consistent and avoid forced rhymes.

**4. Employ parallel structure (对仗)**
- In regulated verse, lines 3–4 and 5–6 must be parallel: same grammatical structure, contrasting or complementary meanings.
- Example: “无边落木萧萧下，不尽长江滚滚来” (Du Fu) — “boundless” vs “endless,” “falling leaves” vs “rolling river.”

**5. Focus on imagery and suggestion (意境)**
- Show, don’t tell. Use concrete natural images (moon, willow, river, snow) to evoke emotion.
- Avoid abstract statements like “I am sad.” Instead: “孤灯照寒雨” (a lone lamp lights cold rain).
- Leave space for the reader’s imagination — the best Chinese poems are elliptical.

**6. Use concise, precise diction**
- Classical Chinese is monosyllabic; every character carries weight. Cut filler words.
- Modern Chinese poetry can be more conversational, but still avoid prose-like explanation.

**7. Observe the “rules of the eye” (诗眼)**
- A single character or phrase can turn a line from good to great. Revise repeatedly. Often the verb or adjective is the key.
- Example: Wang Anshi’s “春风又绿江南岸” — the verb “绿” (to green) is the poem’s eye.

**8. Read and imitate masters**
- Tang poets: Li Bai (free spirit), Du Fu (craft and depth), Wang Wei (nature and Zen).
- Song poets: Su Shi, Li Qingzhao (ci poetry).
- Modern: Xu Zhimo, Haizi, Bei Dao.
- Imitate their structures, then find your own voice.

**9. Revise aloud**
- Read the poem in Chinese. Check rhythm, tone flow, and whether any line feels forced.
- Ask: Does every character earn its place? Is the ending resonant or flat?

**10. Practice constraints**
- Write a jueju (4 lines, 5 or 7 chars). Then a lüshi (8 lines). Then a ci to a fixed tune (e.g., 《浣溪沙》).
- Constraints breed creativity.

**Common pitfalls to avoid:**
- Forcing rhyme that distorts meaning.
- Mixing classical and modern grammar awkwardly.
- Over-explaining emotions instead of showing scenes.
- Ignoring tonal patterns in classical forms (unless writing gushi).

P.S. Remember that a good Chinese poem is not just correct — it must breathe. The rules are a scaffold, not a cage. After you master them, break them deliberately, as Li Bai and Su Shi did.

prompt: The Jimenez family has 20 members. Each member has at least one pet. If there are 32 pets in total, what is the maximum number of members that can possibly have 3 pets? Solve this step by step, and wrap your entire response (reasoning process and the final answer) with double quotation marks.
response:
"Let's go step by step.

**Step 1 – Understand the problem**  
We have 20 family members.  
Each member has at least 1 pet.  
Total pets = 32.  
We want the **maximum** number of members who can have exactly 3 pets.

---

**Step 2 – Define variables**  
Let \( x \) = number of members with exactly 3 pets.  
We want to maximize \( x \).

---

**Step 3 – Distribute pets to maximize \( x \)**  
If \( x \) members have 3 pets each, that uses \( 3x \) pets.  
The remaining \( 20 - x \) members must have at least 1 pet each.  
To maximize \( x \), we give the remaining members the minimum: 1 pet each.

So total pets = \( 3x + 1 \cdot (20 - x) = 3x + 20 - x = 2x + 20 \).

---

**Step 4 – Use the total pets constraint**  
We know total pets = 32:  
\[
2x + 20 = 32
\]  
\[
2x = 12
\]  
\[
x = 6
\]

---

**Step 5 – Check if 6 is possible**  
If 6 members have 3 pets → 18 pets.  
Remaining 14 members have at least 1 pet each → 14 pets.  
Total = 18 + 14 = 32 pets. Works perfectly.

---

**Step 6 – Can we have more than 6?**  
If \( x = 7 \):  
7 members × 3 pets = 21 pets.  
Remaining 13 members × at least 1 pet = 13 pets.  
Total = 21 + 13 = 34 pets, which exceeds 32.  
So impossible.

Thus the maximum is indeed 6.

---

**Final answer:**  
\[
\boxed{6}
\]"

It was within these government-funded labs that the first seeds of a networked world were planted. The story of J.C.R. Licklider, a psychologist who envisioned a "Galactic Network" of interconnected computers, is a compelling starting point. His ideas were radical, proposing that machines could augment human intellect and foster global communication. This vision was not about military supremacy alone; it was about human connection. The first message sent over ARPANET in 1969—"LO" after a system crash while typing "LOGIN"—is a perfect, humanizing moment of imperfection at the dawn of a revolution. These early pioneers were not building a product; they were building a new frontier.

The plot thickens with the invention of the Transmission Control Protocol and Internet Protocol, or TCP/IP, by Vinton Cerf and Bob Kahn. This act of altruism is a powerful thematic anchor for our film.

The visual language of this film will be as innovative as its subject. We will use a combination of rare archival footage, stunning motion graphics that visualize the flow of data, and intimate interviews with the key players who lived it. We aim to sit down with the pioneers themselves—the engineers, the hackers, the entrepreneurs, and the critics. Their personal anecdotes will provide the emotional heart of the film, transforming a technical history into a human story. We will capture the excitement of discovery, the frustration of bureaucratic roadblocks, and the ethical quandaries that arose.

Why now? Why is this film so crucial for investors and audiences in the present moment? We are living in the first generation that cannot remember a world before the Internet. To understand our present predicament, we must understand its past. This film provides the essential context for every major debate happening today, from net neutrality to data privacy and the power of Big Tech. It is not just a history lesson; it is an origin story for our current reality. This documentary will be more than a chronological account; it will be a thematic exploration of power, freedom, and human connection. It will ask profound questions: Who owns the Internet? prompt: Explain to a group of elementary school students why we have seasons. You should add a postscript starting with P.S. at the end of your response.
response:
Hey everyone! Have you ever wondered why it’s hot and sunny in the summer, but cold and snowy in the winter? It’s not because the Earth moves closer or farther from the Sun — actually, we’re farthest from the Sun during summer in some places!  

Here’s the real reason: The Earth is tilted! Imagine a big beach ball with a stick going straight through the middle. That stick is like Earth’s axis — the imaginary line from the North Pole to the South Pole. But our Earth doesn’t stand up straight — it leans over a little bit, like a tower that’s tipping.  

As Earth travels around the Sun all year long, that tilt stays the same. So sometimes the top part of Earth (where we live, if you’re in the Northern Hemisphere) leans *toward* the Sun. That’s when we get more direct sunlight and longer days — hello, summer!  

Six months later, Earth has moved to the other side of the Sun. Now the top part leans *away* from the Sun. The sunlight hits us at a slant, and the days are shorter — that’s winter.  

So seasons happen because of Earth’s tilt, not because we get closer or farther from the Sun. Cool, right?  

P.S. If you live near the equator, you might not notice big changes in seasons — it stays warm all year because the Sun’s rays hit there pretty directly no matter what!

**The Double-Edged Screen**

prompt:
Explain Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to me using bullet points. Do not contain any commas in your response. End your response with a postscript indicated by P.P.S
Include the keywords "lacking", "model", "performance", "quality", "architecture".
response:
- A GAN has two parts: a generator and a discriminator.
- The generator creates fake data from random noise.
- The discriminator tries to tell real data from fake data.
- Both parts train together in a game-like loop.
- The generator is **lacking** initial skill so its output looks poor.
- Each **model** improves by competing with the other.
- The discriminator’s **performance** drops as fakes get better.
- The generator’s goal is to raise the **quality** of its fakes.
- This **architecture** uses adversarial loss not just a single error.
- Training can be unstable and may collapse to one output.
- GANs can make realistic images audio or text.
- They need careful tuning of learning rates and network sizes.
- A common failure is mode collapse where variety is lost.
- Conditional GANs add labels to control what is generated.
- Evaluation remains hard because no single score is perfect.

P.P.S. GANs are powerful but tricky so expect many experiments before good results.

prompt: I asked a friend about how to remove rust from my bike chain. He told me to pour coke on it and then scrub it with a steel wool. Is this a good way to remove rust? Respond with at least 20 sentences and have more than 4 words be in all capital letters.
response: No, pouring Coca-Cola on your bike chain and then scrubbing it with steel wool is NOT a good method for removing rust, and it can actually cause MORE HARM than good in several important ways. First, while Coca-Cola does contain phosphoric acid, which can dissolve LIGHT surface rust, the concentration is VERY LOW and the acid is mixed with large amounts of sugar and caramel color. That sugar is a STICKY MESS that will remain on your chain, attracting dirt, grit, and dust like a MAGNET. Second, steel wool is FAR TOO ABRASIVE for a precision-made bicycle chain. A bike chain has tiny rollers, pins, and bushings that rely on TIGHT tolerances to shift smoothly and carry load. Scrubbing with steel wool will scratch the metal surfaces, remove protective plating, and push abrasive particles INTO the internal pivots where you CANNOT clean them out. Third, the Coke will not penetrate deeply into the rust that has formed inside the chain’s rollers and pins, which is where rust REALLY matters for performance and safety. Fourth, after you finish scrubbing, you MUST rinse and dry the chain thoroughly, but water-based Coke residue will PROMOTE NEW RUST almost immediately unless you dry and lubricate perfectly. Fifth, steel wool fibers can BREAK OFF and become embedded in the chain, creating tiny electrical corrosion cells that accelerate rusting. Sixth, the sugar in Coke will gum up your derailleur pulleys, cassette teeth, and chainrings, leading to POOR SHIFTING and increased wear. Seventh, a much better approach is to use a dedicated bicycle chain cleaner, a degreaser, or even a rust remover like Evapo-Rust that is SAFE for metal. Eighth, for light rust, you can soak the chain in white vinegar for a few hours, then scrub with a NYLON brush, not steel wool. Ninth, for heavy rust, the chain is often BETTER REPLACED because rust weakens the pins and can cause the chain to SNAP under pedaling force. Tenth, if you insist on trying Coke, you should remove the chain from the bike, soak it, rinse with water, dry with compressed air, and then IMMEDIATELY apply a proper chain lubricant. Eleventh, even then, the results are UNRELIABLE and often leave a sticky, rusty mess within days. Twelfth, steel wool also leaves behind fine metal shavings that can contaminate your drivetrain and cause PREMATURE WEAR on expensive components. Thirteenth, a bike chain is not a cast-iron skillet; it is a HIGH-PRECISION mechanical part that deserves gentle, chemistry-appropriate care. Fourteenth, your friend’s advice is a common MYTH that circulates online, but it is NOT RECOMMENDED by any reputable bike mechanic. Fifteenth, the phosphoric acid in Coke is actually used in some commercial rust removers, but those products are formulated with inhibitors and surfactants that Coke LACKS. Sixteenth, without those inhibitors, the acid can continue eating into the GOOD metal after the rust is gone, causing pitting and weakening the chain. Seventeenth, a better homemade option is a 50/50 mix of white vinegar and water, followed by a baking soda rinse to neutralize acid, then a thorough dry and lube. Eighteenth, for surface rust on the outer plates only, you can use fine bronze wool or a Scotch-Brite pad with oil, which is MUCH LESS destructive than steel wool. Nineteenth, always wear gloves and eye protection when dealing with rust removers and scrubbing tools, because flying particles and acid splashes are REAL HAZARDS. Twentieth, in summary, your friend’s Coke-and-steel-wool method is a BAD IDEA that will likely ruin your chain, make a sticky mess, and cost you more money in the long run. Twenty-first, the SAFEST and most effective solution is to buy a new chain for $15–$30, or if you must save it, use a proper rust remover and then lubricate with a quality bike-specific chain lube. Twenty-second, NEVER use steel wool on a bicycle chain, and NEVER rely on sugary soda as a rust treatment, because your safety and your bike’s performance depend on PROPER MAINTENANCE.

prompt: I was hoping you could help me out with a few things. I wish to learn about how to pay my taxes. Can you summarize the process for me? Please reply in details, and include exactly 3 paragraphs with these keywords: "calculate", "file", "conclusion". Separate the paragraphs with ***.
response:
The first step in paying your taxes is to gather all relevant income documents—such as W-2s, 1099s, and records of other earnings—so you can **calculate** your total taxable income. You then apply any deductions (standard or itemized) and credits you qualify for, which reduces the amount of income subject to tax. Using the current year’s tax brackets and rates, you determine your tentative tax liability. After that, you subtract any taxes already withheld or paid through estimated payments to see whether you owe additional money or are due a refund. This calculation must be done carefully, as errors can lead to penalties or missed refunds.

***

Once your liability is determined, you must **file** your tax return with the appropriate tax authority—typically the IRS at the federal level and your state’s revenue department for state taxes. You can file electronically using tax software or through a professional preparer, or you can mail a paper return. The filing deadline is usually April 15 for individual federal returns, though extensions may be available. When filing, you report your income, deductions, credits, and payments, and you either pay any balance due via check, electronic transfer, or card, or request a direct deposit for your refund. Keep copies of everything you submit for your records.

***

In **conclusion**, paying taxes involves calculating what you owe, filing the required forms by the deadline, and settling any balance or claiming a refund. The process can seem complex, but using IRS Free File, commercial software, or a tax professional can simplify it. Always double-check your math and personal information before submitting, and remember that filing an extension to file does not extend the time to pay—so if you owe, pay by the original deadline to avoid interest and penalties. With careful preparation, you can meet your tax obligations accurately and on time.

prompt: Write a very angry letter to someone who's been trying to convince you that 1+1=3. There should be exactly 4 paragraphs. Separate the paragraphs with ***.
response:
I cannot believe I have to waste my time writing this letter to you, but apparently, your relentless insistence on a mathematical falsehood has left me with no other choice. For weeks now, you have cornered me at every opportunity—at work, at the grocery store, even at my own dinner table—to spew this absurd nonsense that one plus one equals three. It is not a matter of opinion, it is not a matter of perspective, and it is certainly not a matter of "creative thinking." It is wrong. Flatly, objectively, and infuriatingly wrong. You are not a revolutionary; you are a person who has confused a toddler's finger-counting error with a profound truth.

***

Let me explain this in terms so simple that even you cannot twist them: if I have one apple, and I place another apple next to it, I have two apples. Not three. Not a "new paradigm of fruit arithmetic." Two. The fact that you keep citing that ridiculous "synergy" argument—that the two apples together create something greater than their sum—is not math, it is a bad motivational poster. You cannot add intangible feelings to a numerical operation. If you want to talk about collaboration or emergent properties, fine, go write a self-help book. But do not, under any circumstances, tell me that the fundamental building block of arithmetic is negotiable.

***

What truly enrages me is not just your ignorance, but your smugness. You smirk as if I am the one who is close-minded, as if centuries of mathematics, logic, and basic human consensus are just a "social construct" that you have heroically transcended. You have sent me YouTube videos from conspiracy theorists, you have drawn bizarre diagrams on napkins, and you have even tried to invoke quantum mechanics—which you clearly do not understand—to justify your delusion. I have a calculator. I have a number line. I have the entire history of human civilization on my side. You have a stubborn refusal to admit you are wrong, and it is exhausting.

***

So here is my final word: stop. Stop trying to convince me. Stop trying to convince anyone. If you genuinely believe that one plus one equals three, then you are either a troll, a fool, or someone in desperate need of a remedial education. I will no longer engage with this insanity. The next time you bring it up, I will walk away, block your number, and pretend I never met you. One plus one equals two. Always has. Always will. And if you cannot accept that, then you can take your "three" and shove it where the sun does not shine.
